## Definition

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

If $L=(\ell_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with every diagonal entry
$\ell_{ii}\ne 0$, the **forward substitution solve** of $Lx=b$ is the recursive
construction

$$x_i:=\frac{1}{\ell_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j<i}\ell_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(0\le i<n).$$If $U=(u_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with every diagonal entry $u_{ii}\ne 0$, the **backward substitution solve** of $Ux=b$ is the recursive construction$$x_i:=\frac{1}{u_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j>i}u_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(n-1\ge i\ge 0).$$

The triangular vocabulary is from
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The matrix
product convention from [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] is the one
used when later items rewrite these recursions as matrix equations.

## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

## Definition

At each precision, let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be an instance of [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]] specialized to a finite binary format of integer precision $p\ge2$ and integer normal-exponent bounds $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$. Its normal values are $\pm m2^{j-p+1}$ for integers $2^{p-1}\le m<2^p$ and $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$, with $N_{\min}=2^{j_{\min}}$ and $N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{j_{\max}-p+1}$. The rounding rule is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even by the parity of the normalized significand. Each precision in a mixed-precision procedure has its own format, range, and valid unit-roundoff bound. On every real exact result that is zero or normal, $\operatorname{fl}$ uses this rule; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range $x$, $\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{x})$ is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression $ab+c$; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex
Hilbert spaces and let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For
$\lambda>0$, define

$$B_\lambda:=A^*A+\lambda I_X.$$

Then $B_\lambda:X\to X$ is bijective and

$$\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le\frac1\lambda.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, real or complex Hilbert spaces $X,Y$, a bounded linear map $A:X\to Y$, its Hilbert adjoint $A^*$, and a real $\lambda>0$.

[F1] [[def-hilbert-space]]: A Hilbert space is an inner-product space complete for the norm induced by its inner product.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice states that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F2] [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]: Under Countable Choice, the adjoint assigns to each $y$ the unique vector $A^*y$ satisfying $\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_X$.

[F3] [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]: A linear map is bounded when some finite $C\ge0$ satisfies $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for every $x$.

[F4] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: For vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$.

[F5] [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]: Under Countable Choice, a closed linear subspace $M$ of a Hilbert space satisfies $H=M\oplus M^\perp$.

[F6] [[def-inner-product-space]]: The inner product is linear in its first argument, conjugate symmetric, and positive definite.

[F7] [[def-operator-norm]]: The operator norm is the supremum of $\|Tx\|$ over vectors satisfying $\|x\|\le1$.

[F8] [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]: A vector $z$ lies in $M^\perp$ exactly when $\langle z,m\rangle=0$ for every $m\in M$.

[F9] [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]: The induced norm satisfies $\|v\|^2=\langle v,v\rangle$.

## Proof

1.1 Uniqueness in [F2] gives linearity of $A^*$: for scalars $a,b$ and $y_1,y_2\in Y$, conjugate-linearity of the second slot shows that $aA^*y_1+bA^*y_2$ satisfies the defining identity for $ay_1+by_2$, so it equals $A^*(ay_1+by_2)$. For $w=A^*y$, [F2], [F4] and [F7] give $\|w\|^2=\langle Aw,y\rangle\le|\langle Aw,y\rangle|\le\|A\|\|w\|\|y\|$. Dividing when $w\ne0$, and treating $w=0$ directly, proves $\|A^*y\|\le\|A\|\|y\|$. Thus $A^*$ is bounded, and composition and addition make $B_\lambda$ linear and bounded with $\|B_\lambda x\|\le(\|A\|^2+\lambda)\|x\|$. The adjoint identity and conjugate symmetry [F6] give $\langle B_\lambda x,z\rangle=\langle Ax,Az\rangle+\lambda\langle x,z\rangle=\langle x,B_\lambda z\rangle$ for all $x,z\in X$. In particular, $\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle=\|Ax\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2\ge\lambda\|x\|^2$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F7, F9, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $\|B_\lambda x\|\,\|x\|\ge |\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle|=\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle\ge \lambda\|x\|^2$. Thus $\|B_\lambda x\|\ge\lambda\|x\|$ for $x\ne0$; the same inequality is trivial for $x=0$. Hence $B_\lambda$ is injective. If $B_\lambda x_n$ converges, this inequality applied to $x_n-x_m$ makes $(x_n)$ Cauchy; completeness of $X$ and boundedness of $B_\lambda$ show its limit lies in $\operatorname{ran}B_\lambda$. Therefore the range is closed. [given, F1, F4, F9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $z\in(\operatorname{ran}B_\lambda)^\perp$, [F8] gives $\langle z,B_\lambda x\rangle=0$ for every $x\in X$. By conjugate symmetry [F6] this is $\langle B_\lambda x,z\rangle=0$, and the symmetry identity from step 1.1 gives $\langle x,B_\lambda z\rangle=0$ for every $x\in X$. Taking $x=B_\lambda z$ and using positive definiteness [F6] yields $B_\lambda z=0$; injectivity from step 2.1 then gives $z=0$. Thus the closed range has zero orthogonal complement. [F6, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F5] and the Countable Choice assumption [A1], a closed subspace with zero orthogonal complement is all of $X$; so $B_\lambda$ is surjective as well as injective. For $y=B_\lambda x$, step 2.1 gives $\|B_\lambda^{-1}y\|=\|x\|\le\|y\|/\lambda$, proving $\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le1/\lambda$. [A1, F5, F7, step 2.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For $\lambda>0$, put
$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*$, which is well-defined by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Then for every $g\in Y$,

$$\|R_\lambda g\|\le\frac{\|g\|}{2\sqrt\lambda},\qquad \|R_\lambda\|\le\frac1{2\sqrt\lambda}.$$

The proof uses the normal equation and the Hilbert-space inner product; it
does not use a compact-operator convergence rate or a source condition.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, Hilbert spaces $X,Y$, a bounded linear map $A:X\to Y$, its Hilbert adjoint $A^*$, $\lambda>0$, and $g\in Y$.

[F1] [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]: For $B_\lambda=A^*A+\lambda I_X$, the inverse exists and $\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le1/\lambda$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is the choice assumption used to define the Hilbert adjoint in this argument; full Choice is not used.

[F2] [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]: The adjoint satisfies $\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_X$.

[F3] [[def-inner-product-space]]: The inner product is linear in its first argument and conjugate symmetric.

[F4] [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]: The induced norm satisfies $\|v\|^2=\langle v,v\rangle$.

[F5] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$.

[F6] [[def-operator-norm]]: For bounded $T$, its operator norm is the supremum of $\|Tz\|$ over $\|z\|\le1$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $x=R_\lambda g$. Under [A1], [F2] gives the Hilbert adjoint used in the definition of $R_\lambda$. By [F1], $(A^*A+\lambda I_X)x=A^*g$. Pairing with $x$ and using [F2] gives $\langle A^*Ax,x\rangle_X=\langle Ax,Ax\rangle_Y=\|Ax\|^2$ and $\langle A^*g,x\rangle_X=\langle g,Ax\rangle_Y$ by [F2]–[F4]. Hence $\|Ax\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2=\langle g,Ax\rangle_Y$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 The left side of step 1.1 is real and nonnegative. By [F5], with $s=\|Ax\|$ and $t=\|g\|$, step 1.1 gives $\lambda\|x\|^2=\langle g,Ax\rangle-s^2\le |\langle g,Ax\rangle|-s^2\le ts-s^2$. Completing the square gives $ts-s^2=\frac{t^2}{4}-(s-t/2)^2\le t^2/4$. Since $\lambda>0$, taking nonnegative square roots yields $\|R_\lambda g\|=\|x\|\le\|g\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. [F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The pointwise inequality of step 2.1 holds for every $g\in Y$. Taking the supremum over the unit ball in [F6] gives $\|R_\lambda\|\le1/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. [F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces, let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact (hence bounded), and let $A_h:X\to Y$ be a bounded
discrete operator whose range is a finite-dimensional subspace of $Y$. For
$\lambda>0$,
define

$$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*,\qquad R_{\lambda,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A_h^*.$$

These maps are well-defined by [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Let $x^\dagger\in X$, $y=Ax^\dagger$, $y_\delta=y+e$ with $\|e\|\le\delta$ and $\delta\ge0$, and let $\widetilde x\in X$. Define the exact discrete normal-equation residual

$$r_h=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x-A_h^*y_\delta.$$

Then the following chain is exact:

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +(R_\lambda y_\delta-R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta) +(R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x).$$

Its norm satisfies

$$\|x^\dagger-\widetilde x\|\le \|x^\dagger-R_\lambda y\|+\frac{\delta}{2\sqrt\lambda} +\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_\delta\|+\frac{\|r_h\|}{\lambda}.$$

The first term is regularization bias, the second is data noise, the third is the regularized-operator discretization difference, and the fourth is the solve residual. The third term receives a numerical bound only when an operator-perturbation bound is supplied: if $\|R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h}\|\le\eta_{\lambda,h}$, it is at most $\eta_{\lambda,h}\|y_\delta\|$. If residual evaluation returns $\widehat r_h$ with a certified $\|r_h-\widehat r_h\|\le\rho_h$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_h\|+\rho_h)/\lambda$. If an algorithm has a specified exact-arithmetic stopping output $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ and returns a computed output $\widetilde x$, the last difference can further split as

$$R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x= (R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-x_{\mathrm{stop}}) +(x_{\mathrm{stop}}-\widetilde x).$$

Writing $r_{\mathrm{stop}}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)x_{\mathrm{stop}} -A_h^*y_\delta$, the first term is at most $\|r_{\mathrm{stop}}\|/\lambda$; the second is the separate returned-output roundoff term. Any bound on that roundoff or on residual-evaluation error requires its own arithmetic hypotheses. For a discretized datum $y_{h,\delta}=A_hx^\dagger+e$ formed before inversion, put $d_h=(A-A_h)x^\dagger=y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}$. Let $\widetilde x_h\in X$ be a computed discrete output. The corresponding exact refinement is

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x_h=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +R_\lambda d_h+(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_{h,\delta} +(R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h),$$

so the forward residual discarded by quadrature or collocation is counted before inversion as $R_\lambda d_h$, with $\|R_\lambda d_h\|\le\|d_h\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. The separate operator discretization and solve terms remain. For this refined chain, define $r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x_h-A_h^*y_{h,\delta}$; then $\|R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}-\widetilde x_h\|\le\|r_{h,h}\|/\lambda$. If its evaluation returns $\widehat r_{h,h}$ with a certified $\|r_{h,h}-\widehat r_{h,h}\|\le\rho_{h,h}$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_{h,h}\|+\rho_{h,h})/\lambda$. No rate for $d_h$, no operator perturbation estimate, and no floating-point residual bound is implicit. When $X,Y$ are finite-dimensional and $b=Ax^\dagger+e$, the same identity is the canonical Tikhonov bias/noise formula

$$x^\dagger-A^\#_\lambda b=(I-A^\#_\lambda A)x^\dagger-A^\#_\lambda e, \qquad A^\#_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*.$$

Here $\lambda$ is the coefficient of $\|x\|^2$ in
$\|Ax-b\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2$.

For stored finite matrices, [[lem-computed-augmented-tikhonov-solve-residual-and-output-error]] supplies the concrete augmented-QR or independently certified-residual application: take its $\rho$ as $\rho_h$ with datum $y_\delta$, or as $\rho_{h,h}$ with datum $y_{h,\delta}$. It bounds returned-output roundoff for the exact direct-solve target and retains explicit real/complex realization, square-root representation, successful-operation and nonsingularity conditions.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, real or complex Hilbert spaces $X,Y$, bounded operators $A,A_h:X\to Y$, $A_h$ of finite rank, $x^\dagger\in X$, $e\in Y$, $\lambda>0$, $\delta\ge0$, $\|e\|\le\delta$, and the exact residual $r_h$. For the refined chain also take $\widetilde x_h\in X$ and its exact residual $r_{h,h}$ as defined in the Statement. If evaluated residuals are used, assume the stated certified bounds $\rho_h,\rho_{h,h}$. For the optional stopping/roundoff split, assume the algorithm's specified exact-arithmetic output $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ exists.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: The Hilbert-adjoint definition used here assumes Countable Choice; no use of full Choice is claimed.

[F1] [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]: For a bounded map $T$ between Hilbert spaces and $\lambda>0$, $(T^*T+\lambda I)^{-1}$ exists and has norm at most $1/\lambda$.

[F2] [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-noise-amplification-bound]]: For bounded $T$ and $g$ in its codomain, $R_\lambda g=(T^*T+\lambda I)^{-1}T^*g$ satisfies $\|R_\lambda g\|\le\|g\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$.

[F3] [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]: The adjoint satisfies $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$.

[F4] [[def-operator-norm]]: The operator norm bounds every image by $\|Tz\|\le\|T\|\,\|z\|$.

[F5] [[def-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares]]: For a finite matrix, the regularized objective is $\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$ with $\lambda>0$.

[F6] [[thm-tikhonov-regularised-least-squares-has-a-unique-minimiser]]: Its unique minimizer is $(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b$.

[F7] [[def-compact-linear-operator]]: A compact operator maps bounded sets to sets with compact closure; every compact operator is bounded.

[F8] [[def-hilbert-space]]: A real or complex Hilbert space is an inner-product space complete in the norm induced by its inner product.

[F9] [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]: The induced norm satisfies $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$.

[F10] [[lem-computed-augmented-tikhonov-solve-residual-and-output-error]]: Finite stored real/complex data admit the stated normal-residual certificate and augmented-QR returned-output bound, with all arithmetic and representation hypotheses explicit.

## Proof

1.1 By [F7], $A$ is bounded, and [F8] supplies the Hilbert-space hypotheses. By [F1], both shifted normal operators are invertible, so the displayed $R_\lambda$ and $R_{\lambda,h}$ are defined. Multiplying their definitions by their normal operators gives $(A^*A+\lambda I)R_\lambda=A^*$ and $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)R_{\lambda,h}=A_h^*$. [given, A1, F1, F3, F7, F8, algebra]

1.2 Adding and subtracting the intermediate vectors $R_\lambda y$, $R_\lambda y_\delta$, and $R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$ cancels the intervening terms and proves the stated four-term identity. Since $y_\delta=y+e$, [F2] gives $\|R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta\|=\|R_\lambda e\| \le\delta/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. [given, F2, algebra]

1.3 Adding and subtracting $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ gives the optional stopping/roundoff identity. The normal equation for $R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$ and the definition of $r_{\mathrm{stop}}$ imply $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(x_{\mathrm{stop}}-R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta) =r_{\mathrm{stop}}$. By [F1], the stopping term is at most $\|r_{\mathrm{stop}}\|/\lambda$; the other term is exactly the stated roundoff difference. [given, F1, algebra]

1.4 In the refined datum case, $y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}=(Ax^\dagger+e)-(A_hx^\dagger+e)=d_h$. Inserting $R_\lambda y_{h,\delta}$ and $R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}$ into the chain therefore gives the displayed five-term identity by cancellation. [given, F3, algebra]

2.1 Let $z=R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$. The normal equation in step 1.1 gives $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(\widetilde x-z)=r_h$. By [F1], $\|\widetilde x-z\|\le\|r_h\|/\lambda$. The triangle inequality [F9] applied to the four-term identity, using step 1.2 for its noise term, proves the stated total error bound. [F1, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Applying [F2] to $d_h$ bounds its pre-inversion contribution by $\|R_\lambda d_h\|\le\|d_h\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. Applying [F1] to $r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(\widetilde x_h-R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta})$ gives the stated refined solve-residual bound. Under the residual-evaluation hypothesis, the triangle inequality [F9] gives $\|r_{h,h}\|\le\|\widehat r_{h,h}\|+\rho_{h,h}$. [F1, F2, F9, step 1.4, algebra]

2.3 In the finite-matrix case with $A_h=A$ and the exact regularized output $\widetilde x=R_\lambda y_\delta$, [F5]–[F6] identify $R_\lambda$ with the canonical Tikhonov minimizer. The baseline identity from step 1.2 then reduces to the displayed finite-matrix bias/noise formula. [F5, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By [F4], an assumed operator-norm bound $\|R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h}\|\le\eta_{\lambda,h}$ gives $\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_\delta\| \le\eta_{\lambda,h}\|y_\delta\|$. Also, the triangle inequality [F9] gives $\|r_h\|\le\|\widehat r_h\|+\|r_h-\widehat r_h\| \le\|\widehat r_h\|+\rho_h$ under the stated residual-evaluation hypothesis. These are conditional estimates, not automatic stability claims. [given, F4, F9, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For stored finite data, or for supplied isometric coordinates $A_h=VMU^*$ and returned output $U\widehat x$, apply [F10] to the coefficient matrix $M$ (the matrix case uses identity embeddings) and datum $g=y_\delta$ or $g=y_{h,\delta}$. The exact normal residual lifts isometrically to $r_h$ or $r_{h,h}$, with any certified coordinate-data and orthogonal-output allowances from [F10]. Hence steps 2.2 and 3.1 apply. For the exact direct augmented solve, $x_{\mathrm{stop}}=R_{\lambda,h}g$, and [F10] bounds the returned-output term by $(\|\widehat r\|+\rho)/\lambda$. The analytic identity and its independent bias, noise and discretization terms are unchanged. [F10, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

Hansen's slides write the penalty as $\|Ax-b\|^2+\lambda_H^2\|x\|^2$; there $\lambda=\lambda_H^2$. Clason's coefficient $\alpha$ in front of the squared penalty maps directly to this item's $\lambda$. The concrete finite-matrix allowance is supplied by [[lem-computed-augmented-tikhonov-solve-residual-and-output-error]]; for general Hilbert-space computations any residual certificate still needs its own stated arithmetic realization.
